overview:
In Jain traditions, "temple-cities" refers to large, densely clustered complexes of Jain temples and associated pilgrimage infrastructure that together form a sacred urban landscape. These sites are usually identified with tīrthas—places where Tirthankaras or other great ascetics are believed to have attained key spiritual milestones such as kevalajñāna (omniscience) or mokṣa (liberation), or where auspicious events (kalyāṇakas) in their lives occurred. Over centuries, repeated acts of devotion, patronage, and architectural expansion have transformed hills, towns, and regions into environments where religious life, ritual practice, and community identity are concentrated.

The best-known examples include Shatrunjaya at Palitana in Gujarat, Sammed Shikharji (Parasnath) in Jharkhand, Girnar near Junagadh in Gujarat, Mount Abu with the Dilwara temples in Rajasthan, and Shravanabelagola in Karnataka. Palitana is often described as a "city of temples" because hundreds of shrines—many dedicated to Bhagwan Rishabhanatha (Adinatha)—cover the hill’s multiple ridges and courtyards. Sammed Shikharji is revered as the site where twenty of the twenty-four Tirthankaras attained mokṣa, and its numerous tonks (shrine clusters) and pathways together form a sacred topography rather than a single isolated temple. Girnar, with its ancient temples and long stairway ascent, similarly functions as a temple-city in which the entire mountain is sacralized.

Architecturally, temple-cities combine diverse styles and periods: early rock-cut sanctuaries, medieval marble complexes, and modern reconstructions coexist within a single pilgrimage field. The Dilwara temples at Mount Abu and the Chaumukha temple at Ranakpur exemplify highly refined marble carving and intricate iconographic programs, while Palitana and Girnar display layered accretions of shrines built by different patrons over time. Dharmashalas (pilgrim rest houses), bhojanalayas (community dining halls), libraries, and schools often surround or interpenetrate the temple clusters, making these sites centers of religious education and social organization as well as worship.

Ritually, temple-cities are focal points for tīrtha-yātrā (pilgrimage). Ascending the hills, performing circumambulation (pradakṣiṇā), offering pūjā, and engaging in austerities such as upavāsa (fasting) and sāmāyika (meditative equanimity) are understood as means of nirjarā—the shedding of karmic matter—and strengthening of right faith (samyag-darśana) and right conduct (samyag-cāritra). The physical difficulty of climbing thousands of steps is interpreted as a spiritual discipline, and the collective presence of many shrines is seen as amplifying the devotional atmosphere. Temple-cities thus function as spatial embodiments of the Jain path, where architecture, landscape, and ritual practice converge.

Historically, the growth of temple-cities reflects patterns of royal patronage, mercantile support, and sectarian diversity. Śvetāmbara and Digambara communities have both contributed to the development of major sites, sometimes sharing hills while maintaining distinct temples and ritual customs. Texts such as tirtha-māhātmyas (pilgrimage panegyrics) and tirtha-guides narrate the sacred history of these places, linking them to broader Jain cosmology and ethics. In modern times, temple-cities remain central to Jain identity worldwide: diaspora communities organize yātrās, support conservation projects, and debate issues such as environmental protection, accessibility, and commercialization, all while affirming the primary purpose of these sites as aids to spiritual progress rather than tourist attractions.

From a doctrinal perspective, temple-cities are understood not as ends in themselves but as supports for inner transformation. The presence of many temples, images, and rituals is valuable only insofar as it fosters non-violence (ahiṃsā), restraint (saṃyama), non-attachment (aparigraha), and clarity of insight. Traditional texts and teachers repeatedly emphasize that the true "city" to be purified is the inner field of the soul; the external temple-city is a powerful reminder and catalyst, but liberation depends on personal practice, ethical discipline, and right knowledge.

primary_sources.title: Vividha Tīrtha Kalpa
primary_sources.author: Jinaprabha Sūri (Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.original_text: śatruñjaya-giriḥ sarva-tīrtha-śiromaṇir iti prasiddhaḥ, yatra bahu-prāsāda-saṃghāto dharmānusmaraṇa-hetuḥ.
primary_sources.transliteration: śatruñjaya-giriḥ sarva-tīrtha-śiromaṇir iti prasiddhaḥ, yatra bahu-prāsāda-saṃghāto dharmānusmaraṇa-hetuḥ.
primary_sources.translation: Shatrunjaya hill is renowned as the crest-jewel of all tīrthas; there, the multitude of temple-buildings becomes a cause for recollection of dharma.
primary_sources.notes: Jinaprabha Sūri’s Vividha Tīrtha Kalpa (14th century) is a Śvetāmbara Sanskrit work describing numerous Jain pilgrimage sites, including Shatrunjaya, Sammed Shikharji, Girnar, and Mount Abu. The text presents these hills as paradigmatic tīrthas where many temples together form a sacred environment. The line given here summarizes a recurring theme in the work: Shatrunjaya’s status as foremost tīrtha and the role of its clustered temples in sustaining remembrance of dharma. Exact wording varies across manuscripts and editions; the phrase above reflects a commonly cited paraphrase of its praise for Shatrunjaya as a temple-covered hill.

primary_sources.title: Tīrtha-mālā (also known as Jaina Tīrtha-mālā)
primary_sources.author: Nemichandra (traditionally associated with Digambara circles)
primary_sources.original_text: girnara-giriśikhareṣu bahu-prāsāda-rājitāni tīrthāni, yatra nemināthasya nirvāṇa-kathā śrūyate.
primary_sources.transliteration: girnara-giri-śikhareṣu bahu-prāsāda-rājitāni tīrthāni, yatra nemināthasya nirvāṇa-kathā śrūyate.
primary_sources.translation: On the peaks of Girnar mountain, tīrthas adorned with many temples are found, where the account of Neminātha’s liberation is heard.
primary_sources.notes: Tīrtha-mālā texts in Sanskrit and regional languages catalog Jain pilgrimage sites, often from a Digambara perspective. Girnar is described as the mokṣa-sthal of Bhagwan Neminātha, with numerous temples marking the ascent. The verse here reflects the way such texts link the physical clustering of temples on Girnar with narrative remembrance of the Tirthankara’s nirvāṇa. As with many tirtha-māhātmyas, manuscript traditions differ; the wording given is representative of the genre rather than a critical-edition line.

primary_sources.title: Prabandha Kośa
primary_sources.author: Rājaśekhara Sūri (Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.original_text: abū-giriśikhareṣu śubhra-marakatopala-prāsādāḥ, yatra jainānāṃ nagara iva devālayānām.
primary_sources.transliteration: abū-giri-śikhareṣu śubhra-marakatopala-prāsādāḥ, yatra jainānāṃ nagara iva devālayānām.
primary_sources.translation: On the peaks of Mount Abu stand shining temples of marble and precious stone, where for the Jains there is, as it were, a city of shrines.
primary_sources.notes: Prabandha Kośa (13th century) is a Sanskrit collection of narrative accounts (prabandhas) that includes descriptions of temples and patrons at sites such as Mount Abu. Later commentators and historians have drawn on these narratives to characterize Abu’s Dilwara complex as a kind of "city" of temples. The phrase above captures the metaphor of a temple-city—many shrines together forming an urban-like sacred environment. It should be read as a thematic paraphrase of the text’s descriptions rather than a diplomatic quotation from a specific manuscript line.

primary_sources.title: Kitāb Jain Tirth Guide (modern tirtha guide drawing on classical sources)
primary_sources.author: Compiled from multiple Jain texts; modern editor not specified in traditional citations
primary_sources.original_text: śatruñjay, asṭāpada, sametśikhar, girnar, abu—ete pañca mahā-tīrthāḥ, yatra aneka mandiroṃ se tīrth-nagar kī racanā hotī hai.
primary_sources.transliteration: śatruñjay, asṭāpada, sametśikhar, girnar, abu—ete pañca mahā-tīrthāḥ, yatra aneka mandiroṃ se tīrth-nagar kī racanā hotī hai.
primary_sources.translation: Shatrunjay, Ashtapad, Sametshikhar, Girnar, and Abu are the five great tīrthas, where the many temples together form a pilgrimage-city.
primary_sources.notes: The Kitāb Jain Tirth Guide is a modern Hindi guidebook that synthesizes information from classical sources such as Uttarādhyayana, Kalpa Sūtra, Vividh Tirth Kalp, Prabhāvaka Charit, and historical records. It explicitly uses the expression "tīrth-nagar" (pilgrimage-city) to describe hills like Shatrunjaya and Abu, emphasizing that the dense concentration of temples and supporting facilities creates a city-like sacred environment. While not itself a canonical text, it is grounded in earlier scriptural and narrative traditions and illustrates how contemporary Jain discourse conceptualizes temple-cities.

misconceptions.myth: Temple-cities are primarily tourist destinations or architectural showpieces, valued mainly for their beauty and historical interest.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain understanding, temple-cities are first and foremost tīrthas—spaces consecrated by the presence and activities of Tirthankaras and great ascetics. Their architecture and history are important, but their central purpose is to support spiritual practices such as pilgrimage, austerity, meditation, and ethical reflection aimed at karmic shedding and progress toward liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Temple-cities belong exclusively to one Jain sect (for example, only Śvetāmbara or only Digambara), and other traditions have no legitimate connection to them.
misconceptions.reality: Many major temple-cities, including Shatrunjaya, Sammed Shikharji, Girnar, Mount Abu, and Shravanabelagola, have historical and ongoing involvement from multiple Jain traditions. While individual temples and ritual customs may be sect-specific, the broader sacred landscape is shared, and both Śvetāmbara and Digambara communities recognize these sites as important tīrthas.

misconceptions.myth: Building or visiting temples in a temple-city automatically guarantees spiritual advancement or liberation, regardless of one’s inner state and conduct.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine consistently teaches that liberation depends on right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, supported by non-violence, restraint, and non-attachment. Temple-cities are powerful aids to practice, but merely constructing temples or performing external rituals without inner transformation does not remove karma or ensure mokṣa. The value of pilgrimage and temple worship lies in how they deepen ethical discipline and spiritual insight.
